strapline: The Mundubile bail case waits for the DPP, the Speaker settles who leads the opposition, the Auditor-General counts the uncollected — and a must-win in Rabat

stories.title: Another week in Mukobeko: the State opposes bail for Mundubile and 17 others — and the hearing moves to 28 October with the DPP joined, the Zambian Observer reports
stories.excerpt: Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 co-accused came back to the Lusaka High Court on Wednesday 21 October for the constitutional bail hearing that was adjourned on Monday. The State has now filed an affidavit opposing release, arguing that treason cases take time and that the Director of Public Prosecutions must be a party. The Zambian Observer reports that both sides agreed to join Gilbert Phiri and that the hearing now goes to 28 October. The 18 remain in custody in Kabwe.

image.label: The bail file
image.caption: The constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others is before a three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court; the State opposes it.

body: The 18 people detained since the aftermath of the 13 August general election will spend at least another week at Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe. Their application for constitutional bail, which stalled on Monday 19 October when the State said it was not ready, returned to the Lusaka High Court on Wednesday 21 October — and, according to the Zambian Observer, left again with a new date of 28 October and a new respondent, Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri.

The applicants are Brian Mundubile, the NRPUP’s presidential candidate at the August election, his running mate Makebi Zulu, and 16 others. Among those named in the court papers reported by Lusaka Times and Zambia Monitor are former Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, business executive Harry Findley, Patrick Mwansa, lawyer George Chisanga and three former commandos. They face charges that include treason, sedition and offences under the anti-terrorism law, arising from what the authorities describe as an alleged militia operating after the election. Mr Mundubile denies that his party had a militia, Zambia Monitor reported.

The State’s position, filed after Monday’s adjournment, is set out in an affidavit sworn by Assistant Superintendent Saviours Hakumbi of the Zambia Police Service’s Fraud and Cyber Crimes Unit, reported by Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. It denies that the applicants’ constitutional rights have been violated. It argues that treason cases are complex, require extensive investigation and consultation and therefore often take a long time to conclude, and it asks the court to take judicial notice of how long the treason cases of Edward Jack Shamwana, Christon Tembo and Hakainde Hichilema took.

On bail itself, the affidavit says the court should weigh the seriousness of the charges, the risk of flight, public safety and the time already spent in custody. It also contends that Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha and Correctional Service Commissioner General Fredrick Chilukutu are public officers doing their jobs and cannot be sued in their personal capacities, and that a constitutional bail application is criminal in nature and cannot proceed without the DPP as a party. News Diggers lists the original respondents as the Attorney General, Harrington Akushanga and the Commissioner General.

The Zambian Observer, in two reports on Wednesday afternoon, says the matter came before the panel led by Ndola-based High Court Judge Derrick Mulenga, sitting with Judges Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, and that the State and the defence agreed by consent to add Mr Phiri as a respondent and to remove the individuals cited in their personal capacities. Mr Kabesha is reported to have said the application is criminal in nature and that the DPP will respond once the agreement is filed. Defence lawyer Sakwiba Sikota is reported to have said the defence could not oppose the application in the interest of justice, while expressing concern that the accused were brought to court without any explanation from the State. The hearing was set for 28 October. No other outlet had reported Wednesday’s proceedings by the time this edition closed.

Monday’s sitting lasted long enough for Acting Chief State Advocate Chibesa Mulonda to ask for more time to file an opposing affidavit, which the panel granted, according to Lusaka Times and the Times of Zambia. The State was ordered to serve its papers by lunchtime, the defence to reply the next day, and arguments were set for Wednesday at 08:30. The accused were not in chambers for the procedural exchange and were briefed by their lawyers in the court cells.
Mr Sikota told journalists that the 18 had been woken at about 04:00 in Kabwe and driven to Lusaka without breakfast, and that the defence had served its summons the previous Thursday.

body.text: We had served the State last Thursday; they have had the documents for a number of days now.
body.attribution: Sakwiba Sikota, State Counsel for the applicants, speaking to journalists at the Lusaka High Court on Monday 19 October, as reported by Lusaka Times

body: Separately, Tonse Alliance secretary general Muhabi Lungu said in an interview on Tuesday that the defence had asked for the detainees to be kept in Lusaka so that lawyers could consult them without travelling to Kabwe, News Diggers reported.

The application, as reported by Lusaka Times when it was filed, accepts that the State is entitled to investigate but says an incomplete investigation cannot justify prolonged detention without judicial proceedings. It relies on a statement attributed to Mr Phiri on 14 September that treason investigations were continuing, cites alleged irregularities over remand warrants, detention conditions and access to medical care, and says that three of the applicants — Ezra Tolopo, Dickson Tembo and Victor Muzyamba — were apprehended at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on 1 August and held at unknown locations for more than nine days. The applicants ask to be released, unconditionally or on conditions, and for a declaration that detention without trial within a reasonable time violates their rights.

body.title: Key dates
items: 1 August — three applicants reportedly apprehended at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport
14 October — constitutional bail application filed, per the Zambian Observer
19 October — hearing adjourned after the State asks for more time
21 October — DPP joined by consent; hearing set for 28 October (Zambian Observer)

body.confirmed: Eighteen applicants including Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu are held at Mukobeko and have applied to the Lusaka High Court for constitutional bail (Lusaka Times, Times of Zambia, Zambia Monitor, News Diggers). The matter is before Judges Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga. Monday’s hearing was adjourned to Wednesday at the State’s request. The State has filed an affidavit by Assistant Superintendent Saviours Hakumbi opposing release and seeking the DPP’s joinder.
body.unverified: Wednesday’s consent order joining DPP Gilbert Phiri, the removal of personally cited respondents and the 28 October date are so far reported only by the Zambian Observer. The 1 August airport detentions and the conditions of transport are the applicants’ and their lawyers’ accounts, not findings of the court. The underlying treason, sedition and terrorism allegations have not been tested; none of the 18 has been convicted of anything.

stories.title: One name, two sets of minutes: the Speaker recognises Ezra Tembo as Leader of the Opposition and ends the Kampyongo claim
stories.excerpt: Speaker Nelly Mutti told the National Assembly on Tuesday 20 October that she had received communication from the NRPUP’s secretary general confirming party president Ezra Tembo as Leader of the Opposition, with Milenge MP Gystave Chonde as Whip and Nyimba North MP Paul Lungu as Deputy Whip. The ruling closes a three-week dispute in which a rival caucus said it had elected Shiwang’andu MP Stephen Kampyongo to the post.

image.label: Leader of the Opposition
image.caption: The Speaker has recognised NRPUP president Ezra Tembo as Leader of the Opposition after a dispute over which party meeting’s minutes counted.

body: The question of who speaks for the opposition benches of the 14th National Assembly was settled from the chair on Tuesday 20 October. Speaker Nelly Mutti informed the House that she had received communication from the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity’s secretary general, Nonde Mubanga, confirming the election of party president Ezra Tembo as Leader of the Opposition, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer reported. She also announced Milenge MP Gystave Chonde as Party Whip and Nyimba North MP Paul Lungu as Deputy Whip.

body.text: Honourable Ezra Tembo is the recognised Leader of the Opposition in Parliament.
body.attribution: Speaker Nelly Mutti, in the National Assembly on Tuesday 20 October, as reported by the Zambian Observer

body: The announcement ends a dispute that had run since late September. According to the NRPUP’s own account, carried by the Zambian Observer on 28 September, 34 of the party’s MPs meeting at Palmwood Lodge on 3 September chose Mr Tembo for the post, on a motion by Luanshya MP Golden Mulenga seconded by Mr Lungu and Chembe MP Chomba Kasongo, and a nomination letter went to the National Assembly. On 27 September a second meeting of NRPUP parliamentarians at a Lusaka lodge was reported to have elected Shiwang’andu MP Stephen Kampyongo instead, citing Article 74(2) of the Constitution, which gives the opposition party with the most seats the right to choose the Leader of the Opposition. The party said the September decision could not be overturned unilaterally by another meeting; Mr Kampyongo had indicated that fellow MPs had elected him, News Diggers reported.

body.text: What the ruling does and does not settle

body: The Speaker’s statement rested on the communication from the party’s secretary general, not on a judgement about which caucus was better attended. The Zambian Observer reports that Mr Tembo has insisted all of the party’s lawmakers owe their loyalty to the party leadership — it puts the number at 59 — and describes managing divisions within his own ranks as his first task. Mr Kampyongo’s response to Tuesday’s announcement had not been reported by the outlets reviewed for this edition.

The post carries practical weight: the Leader of the Opposition directs the largest opposition bloc’s legislative strategy and its responses to government business, and the Whip and Deputy Whip organise its votes. Both News Diggers and the Zambian Observer note that the opposition benches had been divided for several weeks between the party leadership and the group that met on 27 September. Whether the second group accepts the Speaker’s ruling, and whether the NRPUP takes any disciplinary step against those who attended the rival meeting, are the questions that follow.

stories.title: ‘A fugitive does not acquire immunity by crossing a border’: State House answers the civil-society groups questioning how Jay Jay Banda was brought home
stories.excerpt: A coalition of civil-society organisations has asked the Zambian and Mozambican governments to account for the cross-border apprehension of former Petauke Central MP Emmanuel ‘Jay Jay’ Banda and to explain how he came to be in a critical condition at Maina Soko Military Hospital. State House, through Clayson Hamasaka, calls the statement a political booby trap and says only bogus organisations could question the arrest of a man who, it says, publicly called for the President’s assassination.

image.label: Across the border
image.caption: Civil-society groups and State House disagree over the legality of the cross-border operation that brought Emmanuel ‘Jay Jay’ Banda back from Mozambique.

body: A week after Emmanuel ‘Jay Jay’ Banda was apprehended in Mozambique on 14 October — an arrest the Zambian authorities have confirmed, according to Zambia Monitor — the argument has moved from whether he was caught to how. A joint statement by a consortium of local and regional civil-society organisations and human-rights defenders, issued on Sunday 18 October, called on Zambia and Mozambique to account for the operation and said that whatever Mr Banda’s past conduct, both governments must still follow the law in his arrest and transfer, News Diggers reported. The signatories listed by News Diggers include the Advocates for Democratic Governance Foundation, Caritas Zambia, Chapter One Foundation, Free Press Initiative Zambia and the LCK Freedom Foundation; the Zambian Observer puts the number of organisations at 24, including groups from South Africa and Botswana.

The statement also asked the authorities to disclose how Mr Banda came to be in a critical condition at Maina Soko Military Hospital, pointing to the government’s duty to protect the life of anyone in its custody.

State House chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka responded on Tuesday 20 October. According to the Zambian Observer, which carried the statement, he described the coalition’s position as a political booby trap designed to turn a fleeing suspect into a martyr, pointed to what he called a contradiction between not declaring the apprehension unlawful and asking the international community to condemn acts of lawlessness, and defended the operation as mutual legal assistance between sovereign states. The statement said Mr Banda is safe in custody, will receive medical care and access to counsel and family, and will be presented before a competent court.

body.text: A fugitive does not acquire immunity by crossing a border.
body.attribution: State House statement issued by Clayson Hamasaka on Tuesday 20 October, as carried by the Zambian Observer

body: News Diggers reports Mr Hamasaka as saying that only bogus organisations could question the apprehension of a suspect who publicly called for the assassination of the Head of State, and that no genuine human-rights defender could excuse such incitement and remain credible. Home Affairs permanent secretary Dickson Matembo asked why the same organisations had not spoken out about Mr Banda’s alleged violations against the President. Two days earlier Mr Hamasaka had called Amnesty International hypocrites after it questioned the operation.

Amnesty International Africa said on 17 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor, that the authorities had confirmed Mr Banda was arrested in Mozambique on 14 October by a joint task force. It asked for a qualified health professional to assess him, for confidential access to a lawyer and his family, and for the legal basis of his detention to be disclosed. It said no one should be transferred to a country where they face a real risk of serious rights violations, and that the authorities should either release him or establish lawful grounds before a competent court.

Mr Banda was arrested in June 2024 and charged with aggravated robbery and attempted murder, according to Lusaka Times. On 4 August 2024 he escaped from Chipata General Hospital, where he was being treated under guard, and the Speaker declared his seat vacant in November 2024 after he ignored a summons to appear. The Zambian Observer reports that the government offered a K2 million bounty. Opposition figures said on 16 October that he had been seized at a hideout in Mozambique; opposition-aligned reports that he had been shot were not confirmed, Lusaka Times noted. He has not been convicted of any offence, and the charges against him are untested in court.

stories.title: K626 million in mining penalties never collected, K3.56 billion owed by the Ministry of Health: the Auditor-General’s account of 2025
stories.excerpt: The Auditor-General’s report on the accounts for the year to 31 December 2025, released by Acting Auditor-General Patricia Malaila, finds that the Ministry of Mines failed to collect K626.64 million in penalties from licence holders, that the Ministry of Health carries K3.56 billion in unpaid obligations some dating to 2014, and that only 27 of 5,595 confiscated mukula logs could be found. Unresolved findings fell from 33 to 27.

image.label: The 2025 audit
image.caption: The Auditor-General’s report for 2025 lists uncollected revenue, unpaid bills and missing assets across ministries and agencies.

body: The Office of the Auditor-General has published its report on the accounts of the Republic for the financial year ended 31 December 2025, and the headline figures are about money owed rather than money stolen. According to Zambia Monitor, Lusaka Times and News Diggers, the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development failed to collect K626.64 million in penalties due from mining licence holders, and a further K30.48 million in annual area charges remained outstanding. The Department of Immigration had not remitted US$433,820 collected on the Treasury’s behalf, and the Zambia Revenue Authority could not account for K41.97 million in customs duties and K9.03 million in temporary imports because supporting documents were missing.

Acting Auditor-General Patricia Malaila said the weaknesses had caused revenue losses and inefficient use of public resources and had reduced the effectiveness of service delivery, Lusaka Times reported.

The largest single figure sits at the Ministry of Health, which the report says has outstanding obligations of K3.56 billion covering employee-related liabilities and unpaid suppliers’ bills, some dating back to 2014.

body.text: The continued growth of these obligations places considerable pressure on public finances
body.attribution: Acting Auditor-General Patricia Malaila, in the report as quoted by Zambia Monitor on 19 October

body: The report warns that the arrears expose the Treasury to penalties, interest and litigation, and notes that Mbala General Hospital was still paying to transport oxygen from other towns. At the Ministry of Education, 125 officers who were paid salaries totalling K1.23 million did not appear on staff returns and were not recognised at their reported stations — an irregularity the report says raises concerns about the integrity of payroll controls. The ministry was also cited for not finishing the printing and distribution of learning materials for the new curriculum.

Under the Farmer Input Support Programme, auditors found irregularities exceeding K72 million involving inactive and unapproved beneficiaries and people drawing on more than one government support scheme. The Ministry of Lands could not assess ground rent on 74,840 properties because its land records are incomplete, and the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation had not secured title deeds for 663 government properties. At the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment, auditors recorded 5,595 confiscated mukula logs but could physically verify only 27, leaving 5,568 unaccounted for.

Ms Malaila said the number of unresolved audit findings had fallen from 33 in 2024 to 27, which she attributed to engagement with controlling officers, while noting that significant gaps remain. She urged controlling officers to implement the report’s recommendations without delay, strengthen internal controls, improve revenue collection, tighten procurement and payroll management, safeguard public assets and recover funds where applicable. None of the ministries named had responded publicly in the reports reviewed.

stories.title: ‘Use it or lose it’, then a regional pitch: Botswana and the DRC bring proposals to the Mining Insaka after Hichilema’s warning to licence-holders
stories.excerpt: On the second day of the Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka at Mulungushi, Botswana’s minerals minister Bogolo Kenewendo and the DRC’s mines minister Louis Watum Kabamba urged shared processing, equipment manufacturing and border and rail cooperation, with a proposed Botswana–Zambia industrial campus tied to a 300 MW solar project. A day earlier President Hichilema told more than 1,300 delegates that tenements must be explored, that the state has spent almost US$100 million on a nationwide geophysical survey, and that the Insaka ‘is not a holiday’.

image.label: Insaka, day two
image.caption: Ministers from Botswana and the DRC set out regional mining proposals at the Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka.

body: The third Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka moved from exhortation to proposals on Tuesday 20 October. Representing President Duma Boko, Botswana’s Minister of Minerals and Energy Bogolo Joy Kenewendo told the gathering at Mulungushi International Conference Centre that Africa must move beyond being a source of raw materials and build industries that process minerals and make mining equipment, Zambia Monitor reported. Botswana and Zambia, she said, could pair their resources, technical expertise and geography in skills development, equipment manufacturing, engineering and regional supply chains, with a possible industrial campus linked to a proposed 300-megawatt solar plant and battery storage facility, subject to commercial and technical assessment.

Speaking for President Félix Tshisekedi, the Democratic Republic of Congo’s mines minister Louis Watum Kabamba pointed to the shared Copperbelt, proposed rail investment to ease border congestion and called for cooperation on geological research and on curbing the illicit minerals trade, according to Zambia Monitor and African Mining Market. Acting Minister of Mines Gilbert Siame — who at Monday’s opening had set a target of three million tonnes of copper a year within five years, according to Lusaka Times — said reforms should be judged by their effect on ordinary Zambians, with more local processing and manufacturing.

President Hakainde Hichilema opened the four-day event on Monday 19 October before more than 1,300 local and foreign delegates, the Times of Zambia reported, and his message was impatience. He said one investor had held a licence for more than 25 years without developing it, that the government now applies a use-it-or-lose-it approach to tenements, and that holders who cannot explore should consider joint ventures with capable partners, Lusaka Times reported.

body.text: We need to agree that tenements must be explored prospectively.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, opening the Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka on Monday 19 October, as reported by the Times of Zambia

body: He told delegates the Insaka was not a holiday but a business, urged them to use the reserved deal rooms in the Kenneth Kaunda wing and to close transactions rather than schedule the next meeting, and said that mining disputes belong in boardrooms, not courtrooms.

The President said the nationwide high-resolution geophysical survey, covering 752,000 square kilometres at a cost to the state of almost US$100 million, would be complete within a month and fills a gap left for 62 years. He cited Luanshya’s 28 Shaft and the Kalengwa mine as idle assets being revived, said Konkola Copper Mines had agreed to contribute 300,000 tonnes towards the national copper target, and put local-content commitments at close to US$1 billion for local suppliers in about a year, with Kansanshi’s US$1.3 billion S3 expansion sourcing cabling, electricals and grinding balls locally. He also said government vehicle purchases would move to electric vehicles where practical and that the next budget would fund a skills centre in each of the 116 districts.

stories.title: Every director sent home: the new ZEMA board orders a 60-day competency audit and installs an interim chief from UNZA
stories.excerpt: Green Economy and Environment Minister Gilbert Siame announced on Tuesday 20 October that the newly constituted board of the Zambia Environmental Management Agency has placed all of the agency’s directors on administrative leave pending assessments of competence and suitability, and appointed Dr Joel Kabika of the University of Zambia as interim director-general for six months. A policy institute has asked for due process and a clear line between the board and management.

image.label: ZEMA clear-out
image.caption: The Zambia Environmental Management Agency’s directors have been placed on administrative leave while a new board assesses them.

body: The Zambia Environmental Management Agency has lost its entire directorate, at least for now. In a statement on Tuesday 20 October reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer, Minister of Green Economy and Environment Gilbert Siame said the newly constituted board had placed all directors at the agency on administrative leave with immediate effect. They will be assessed on competence, performance and suitability, after which the board will decide whether to reinstate or dismiss them; the Zambian Observer puts the audit period at 60 days.

Dr Joel Kabika, an academic at the University of Zambia’s School of Engineering, has been appointed interim director-general for six months, after which the board is expected to advertise the post. Dr Siame said the process would follow the law and that routine services would continue without disruption, and that the realignment is not limited to ZEMA: similar reviews have begun in every department under his ministry to align structures, staffing and operations with performance expectations.

The move follows a run of signals from the ministry. On 19 October Lusaka Times reported that Dr Siame had given the board, chaired by Felix Masiye, until 30 December 2026 to move environmental permitting and licensing fully online, with an integrated application platform, published service standards, real-time tracking and a fast track for low-risk projects, alongside directives on a national carbon registry, forest restoration and climate preparedness. The Zambian Observer attributes the leave decision to frustration from the public and State House, and reports Dr Siame acknowledging that the regulator had not met expectations.

The Action Institute for Policy Analysis Centre responded even before the formal announcement. Its executive director, Solomon Ngoma, said in a statement on Tuesday reported by Zambia Monitor that the institute shared the minister’s concern about degradation and pollution but was troubled by remarks attributed to him suggesting the agency could be dissolved if it failed to prevent mining pollution.

body.text: We sincerely hope the statement was made in frustration over pollution concerns and not as a serious policy position,
body.attribution: Solomon Ngoma, executive director of the Action Institute for Policy Analysis Centre, in a statement in Lusaka on Tuesday 20 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Mr Ngoma said ZEMA has qualified professionals who can do their jobs if allowed to work independently, urged the new board to stay within its statutory mandate rather than interfere in day-to-day operations, and asked that any decisions about directors follow due process. Environmental failures, he said, cannot be attributed to one institution alone. Neither the affected directors nor the board had been reported as responding by the time this edition closed.

stories.title: Six days without a court date: Lima MP Kelvin Kaunda applies for bail from Mwembeshi after a transfer his lawyer says he was not told about
stories.excerpt: Kelvin Kaunda, the NRPUP MP for Lima, was arrested on 15 October on a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm over an incident during the August campaign. He has applied for bail, saying he has been held without being taken before a court; the Correctional Service confirms he has been moved from Lubwa police station to Mwembeshi remand, where his lawyer says he was refused access. His election petition hearing was adjourned on Tuesday because he was not in court.

image.label: Lima MP in custody
image.caption: Lima MP Kelvin Kaunda has applied for bail after being held since 15 October on an assault charge and moved to Mwembeshi remand.

body: The Member of Parliament for Lima, Kelvin Kaunda, has been in custody since Thursday 15 October on a single charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and on Wednesday 21 October News Diggers reported that he had been moved from Lubwa police post to Mwembeshi, where his lawyer, Emmanuel Kaluba, said he was denied access to his client. Zambia Correctional Service spokesman Superintendent Cornelius Mwanza confirmed the transfer, telling the paper: “He is at Mwembeshi Remand.” Mr Kaluba said the police had moved his client to an undisclosed location without informing him.

The charge, under section 248 of the Penal Code, arises from a complaint that a 26-year-old man from Lusaka’s Soweto area was assaulted with stones and fists on Zingalume Road during campaign roadshows at about 19:30 on 7 August, suffering a deep cut to the forehead and a swollen lip, police spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha said in a statement reported by Zambia Monitor on 16 October. Mr Kaunda, 44, of Roma, was described as being in custody awaiting court proceedings. He has not entered a plea and the allegation has not been tested.

Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday that Mr Kaunda has applied for bail pending trial. In an affidavit he says he has been held at Lubwa since 15 October without being brought before a court. His lawyers argue that the offence is bailable, that he has a fixed address in Lusaka and is not a flight risk, that he can provide traceable sureties and will not interfere with witnesses, and that the Criminal Procedure Code requires an arrested person to be taken to court within 24 hours or considered for bond where that is not practicable. The outlet does not name the court hearing the application or report any police response to the custody claims.

The arrest came shortly after the Lusaka High Court adjourned an election petition brought by UPND candidate Lee Mukupa, who alleges electoral malpractice in a contest Mr Kaunda won by 22,760 votes to 8,041, Zambia Monitor reported; the petition hearing was adjourned on Tuesday because Mr Kaunda was not present in court.

body.text: Questions about the length of detention

body: The detention has drawn public comment. Lusaka businessman Chomba Kaoma said on 19 October, as reported by the Zambian Observer, that fellow MPs had submitted sureties and documents for police bond and that the law provides for 48 hours, accusing officers of disregarding the President’s guidance on detentions. Those are his assertions; the police had not responded to them in the reports reviewed.

body.confirmed: Mr Kaunda was arrested on 15 October and charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm (police statement via Zambia Monitor). The Correctional Service confirms he is at Mwembeshi remand (News Diggers). He has filed a bail application (Zambia Monitor). His election petition was adjourned on Tuesday in his absence.
body.unverified: Whether and when he will appear in court on the charge; the reason for the transfer to Mwembeshi; the lawyer’s account of being refused access; and the claim that sureties were lodged and ignored. The assault allegation itself is untested.

stories.title: A summit by video on Wednesday and one in Harare on Thursday: Hichilema’s two days of regional business, and the message he gave the Great Lakes
stories.excerpt: President Hichilema was due to join an extraordinary SADC summit held virtually on Wednesday 21 October to fill treaty positions and elect the next chair of the Organ on Politics, Defence and Security, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe said, before travelling to Harare for the 25th COMESA summit on Thursday 22 October, where Zimbabwe takes the chair from Kenya. On Monday he told a Great Lakes ministerial meeting that hungry populations are hard to govern and that the region should trade food rather than post soldiers.

image.label: Two summits
image.caption: President Hichilema attends a virtual SADC extraordinary summit on Wednesday and the COMESA summit in Harare on Thursday.

body: Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Mulambo Haimbe issued two statements in Lusaka on Wednesday 21 October, one for each of the President’s engagements. The first, reported by Lusaka Times, said President Hakainde Hichilema would take part in an Extraordinary Summit of SADC Heads of State and Government held virtually that day, preceded by a virtual extraordinary meeting of the SADC Council of Ministers. The agenda covers outstanding matters including the filling of treaty positions and the election of the incoming chairperson of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation. Mr Haimbe said the President’s participation underscored Zambia’s commitment to supporting the discussions, strengthening the SADC Secretariat and advancing regional integration, peace and security. No outcome had been reported by the time this edition closed.

The second statement, reported by Zambia Monitor, confirmed that the President will attend the 25th COMESA Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare on Thursday 22 October, hosted by Zimbabwe’s President Emmerson Mnangagwa under the theme ‘One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialisation, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA’. The summit will see the chairmanship pass from Kenya’s William Ruto to Mr Mnangagwa, with a new bureau of Zimbabwe as chair, Eswatini as vice-chair and Kenya as rapporteur. Zambia hosts the COMESA Secretariat in Lusaka and is not part of the bureau changes.

Mr Haimbe linked the trip to the Grow Zambia agenda of expanding trade and attracting investment, and said the President is expected to hold bilateral meetings on the sidelines on trade, investment and development priorities. He said Zambia, as host of the Secretariat, remains firmly committed to the objectives and ideals of COMESA.

The regional round began on Monday 19 October, when the President opened the 20th ordinary session of the Regional Inter-Ministerial Committee of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region in Lusaka — a session Zambia hosted after the Democratic Republic of Congo could not, and which coincides with the 20th anniversary of the Great Lakes Pact on Security, Stability and Development, Lusaka Times reported. News Diggers reported him saying that hungry populations are hard to govern and can turn on those in charge, that countries in the region should trade food with one another rather than station soldiers at border posts, and that leaders should tackle the root causes of conflict by creating opportunities at home — linking migration to Europe to economic conditions in the region.

body.text: You know that Europeans are unhappy with us because a lot of our people are crossing into Europe
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, opening the ICGLR Regional Inter-Ministerial Committee meeting in Lusaka on Monday 19 October, as reported by News Diggers

body.text: We should have non-stop border posts. Technology allows that to happen,
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, at the ICGLR Regional Inter-Ministerial Committee session in Lusaka on Monday 19 October, as reported by Lusaka Times

body: Lusaka Times also reported the President asking what progress had been made by running the region’s meetings the same way for 20 years, and saying that Zambia had not caused the conflict in the region but was suffering its effects. Taken together, the three engagements place Zambia at the table for the region’s security architecture, its largest trading bloc and the Great Lakes process in the same week.

stories.title: ‘A must-win for us’: the Copper Princesses face Venezuela in Rabat tonight after the 5–0 to Japan — and Ken Sekeletu keeps his belt in Tenerife
stories.excerpt: Zambia’s under-17 women play Venezuela at 20:00 CAT on Wednesday 21 October in their second Group D match at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, after losing 5–0 to Japan on the opening day. Both sides are without a point; coach Carol Kanyemba says one defeat is not the end of the tournament and captain Taonga Mubanga has promised a win. In Spain, Ken Sekeletu retained his featherweight title with a third-round stoppage.

image.label: Princesses v Venezuela
image.caption: Zambia’s under-17 women meet Venezuela in Morocco in a match both teams need after opening defeats.

body: The Copper Princesses’ third successive under-17 World Cup began badly and may be decided on its second night. Zambia lost 5–0 to Japan at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in their Group D opener, with Kurita Nanami scoring in the ninth minute from a Hanashiro Mei cross and Oshita Sayana adding a second in the 13th, News Diggers reported. On Wednesday 21 October at 20:00 CAT they meet Venezuela, who lost 2–0 to France, in a match Lusaka Times describes as one that would leave Zambia’s round-of-16 hopes hanging by a thread if it is lost. The game is streamed on FIFA+, ZamFoot reports, with Japan playing France at 17:00 CAT and France waiting for Zambia in the final group match.
Coach Carol Kanyemba, who has taken the side to the 2024, 2025 and 2026 tournaments, has spent the week on morale.

body.text: We have been encouraging the girls that losing one game is not the end of the tournament.
body.attribution: Carol Kanyemba, Zambia under-17 women’s coach, ahead of the Venezuela match, as reported by Lusaka Times on 20 October

body: Captain Taonga Mubanga told ZamFoot the team had worked on the mistakes from the Japan game and that the match was a must-win which would show whether Zambia can reach the last 16; Lusaka Times quotes her as saying the team “will win”. Debutant Dorcas Mulosha said the fixture would motivate the squad. The outlets differ on the tournament format — Lusaka Times says the top two in each group go through with the three best third-placed teams, ZamFoot says four — and this story does not resolve that.

In Spain, Ken Sekeletu retained his featherweight title at the Fight 2 One 12 event in Tenerife on Saturday, stopping Christopher Reyes by technical knockout at 1 minute 42 seconds of the third round after a body shot, strikes and a takedown left the referee no choice, News Diggers reported. The paper says the win follows an earlier technical knockout of Argentina’s Lucas Codutti; it does not name the sanctioning body or give Sekeletu’s full record.
The result from Rabat will be reported in Thursday’s edition. Kick-off is 20:00 CAT.

stories.title: From Matero to the launch stage: Olivia Tutu’s memoir ‘Authentic: A Life Chosen, Not Given’ is launched in Lusaka
stories.excerpt: Olivia Tutu, the 26-year-old founder of Youth on Sustainable Development, launched her ten-chapter memoir in Lusaka on Saturday 17 October, with Absa Bank chief executive Mizinga Melu as guest of honour and UNDP resident representative James Wakiaga among the speakers. The book was published in August and is expected on Amazon in January 2027.

image.label: A life chosen
image.caption: Youth development specialist Olivia Tutu has launched her memoir ‘Authentic: A Life Chosen, Not Given’ in Lusaka.

body: A memoir written at 26 is a statement of intent as much as a record, and Olivia Tutu made hers plain at the launch of ‘Authentic: A Life Chosen, Not Given’ in Lusaka on Saturday 17 October. The ten-chapter book, published in August, traces her path from Matero Township to the founding of Youth on Sustainable Development, work as a development consultant, education activism and speaking engagements abroad, the Times of Zambia reported in a feature on 19 October.

body.text: I do not just want to be a celebrity. I want to matter. I want to leave a mark.
body.attribution: Olivia Tutu, author, at the launch of her memoir in Lusaka on 17 October, as reported by the Times of Zambia

body: She described the book as her most personal work, saying that people had seen the stages, the advocacy and the leadership for years but not the story behind them.

Absa Bank Zambia chief executive Mizinga Melu, the guest of honour, formally launched the book and urged young people to be honest about failure and to write their own stories, saying that a difficult beginning can shape a person without determining where they end up. Dr James Wakiaga, the United Nations Development Programme’s resident representative in Zambia, said giving young people a voice matters and commended the author’s commitment to youth development. A book signing followed; the Times of Zambia quotes an attendee who related to the account of growing up in a village with very little.

The paper describes Ms Tutu as a content creator, technology enthusiast, global speaker and ambassador for the Sustainable Development Goals. It does not name the publisher or give a price, and says the book is expected to be listed on Amazon in January 2027.

For a memoir by a youth-development specialist, the test will be whether the book travels beyond the launch audience into the schools and youth programmes of the kind its author runs; the Amazon listing planned for January would put it in front of readers outside Zambia for the first time.

sources.title: Olivia Tutu launches inspiring memoir in Lusaka

analysis.title: What joining the DPP to the bail case changes — and what it does not
analysis.body: The State’s argument that a constitutional bail application is criminal in nature, and so cannot be decided without the Director of Public Prosecutions, has now been accepted by consent, if the Zambian Observer’s account of Wednesday’s hearing holds. For the applicants that costs another week in Kabwe; for the State it means the prosecutor who said on 14 September that treason investigations were continuing must now answer, on affidavit, why 18 people should stay in custody while they continue. That is the question the panel has been asked to decide, and the affidavit already filed gives the State’s answer: treason cases are long, the charges are grave, and the court should weigh flight risk and public safety. The applicants’ answer is that the Constitution guarantees a court appearance without undue delay, whatever the charge. Two things remain outside the case. The joinder does not bring forward any trial date, and nothing in the bail ruling will say whether the militia allegations are true. Watch 28 October for the DPP’s affidavit, and for whether the court rules from the bench or reserves.

analysis.title: The Speaker chose the secretary general’s letter. The caucus still has to live with it
analysis.body: Speaker Mutti’s route out of the opposition leadership dispute was procedural: she took the party’s formal communication, signed by its secretary general, as decisive. That avoids the harder question of which meeting — 3 September at Palmwood Lodge or 27 September at another Lusaka lodge — better reflected the will of NRPUP MPs, and it leaves Article 74(2) untested, since the Constitution says the largest opposition party elects its leader but not how the House verifies the election. The strongest case for the ruling is that a Speaker cannot referee internal party contests and must rely on the party’s own organs. The strongest case against it, from the group that backed Stephen Kampyongo, is that a party president who is also the parliamentary leader concentrates power that the caucus had tried to share. What follows depends on numbers nobody has published: how many MPs attended the second meeting and whether they now accept the Whip’s instructions. The first contested vote in the House will show whether the opposition speaks with one voice or two.

analysis.title: K626 million uncollected is not theft — which is why it keeps happening
analysis.body: Audit reports attract attention for missing money, but the 2025 report’s biggest numbers are revenue nobody chased and bills nobody paid. The Ministry of Mines did not collect K626.64 million in penalties from licence holders in the same year the President was telling the Mining Insaka that tenements must be explored or surrendered; a penalty that is assessed but not enforced is a weaker signal than one that is. The K3.56 billion owed by the Ministry of Health is a different problem: arrears that go back to 2014 cannot be fixed by a single budget line, and every year they roll forward they attract interest and suppliers’ reluctance. The fall in unresolved findings from 33 to 27 is real progress, but it measures paperwork closed, not kwacha recovered. The next step is parliamentary: the Public Accounts Committee will call controlling officers, and the Treasury will decide whether to clear the health arrears or let them ride. Watch for whether the mining penalties are collected or written off, and whether the 5,568 missing mukula logs produce a prosecution.
